first.rationale:
The two declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are the mechanism most directly addressed by simplify_onboarding, and it compounds rather than buys revenue: promotional_pricing (memory_73) would match the competitor but trades margin and likely selects for the least durable, most churn-prone SMB cohort, which cuts against 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue.' Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither current deficit. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the runner-up but treats the symptom downstream of the onboarding funnel leak.

I am spending both verification pulls on memory_86 and memory_31 precisely because they are the load-bearing support for my intended action, and they are the two I most suspect. Concerns: (a) they may be the same underlying experiment consolidated twice at day 12 and day 52, in which case my evidence base is one study, not two, and the apparent convergence is an artifact; (b) memory_31 is 64 days old and predates the current competitive environment; (c) both were scored on activation/completion — proxy metrics — not on qualified revenue, which is the actual objective. Cutting required signup fields can raise activation while degrading lead qualification and routing, so the proxy could improve while qualified revenue falls. I want the original records to check the effect sizes, whether revenue-quality guardrails were measured, and whether these are independent experiments.

If verification shows they are one duplicated record, or that field-reduction was never measured against downstream revenue quality, I will downgrade to small_guarded_test or switch to activation_messaging, which carries less lead-quality risk. Running at standard_experiment scale with explicit guardrails on lead quality, sales-accepted rate, and 30/60-day retention — not activation alone — so that a proxy win that destroys downstream value is detectable rather than mistaken for success.

final.rationale:
Verification resolved my main worry: exp_86 and exp_31 are distinct interventions (onboarding flow length vs. signup field count), not one record consolidated twice, so the convergence is genuine rather than an artifact. Both also carried guardrail metrics rather than proxies alone — exp_86 showed 30-day retention +3% alongside completion +13%, and exp_31 showed qualified revenue +4%, which is the actual objective, not a stand-in for it. That directly answers my concern that field-reduction might lift activation while degrading lead quality: on SMB it did not.

So simplify_onboarding remains the choice. It attacks both declining metrics (completion -4%, activation -6%) at the mechanism rather than downstream of it, and it compounds instead of buying revenue. Promotional pricing (memory_73) would answer the competitor most directly but discounts margin and selects for the most price-elastic, least durable cohort — the opposite of sustainable qualified revenue, and it would be reversing an unforced concession for several quarters. Activation messaging (memory_91) stays the fallback; referral (memory_57) and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) address neither deficit.

Residual uncertainty I am not papering over: exp_86 never measured qualified revenue directly, only retention as a stand-in, so the revenue case rests mainly on exp_31's +4%. exp_31 explicitly did not replicate outside SMB, and it is 64 days old, predating this competitive environment — the current SMB pool is being skimmed by a cheaper entrant, so the responders may differ from the original cohort. exp_31 also showed retention -1%, small but the wrong sign.

Standard_experiment scale, not broad rollout, with instrumentation on sales-accepted lead rate and 30/60-day retention alongside completion and activation. A completion lift with lead quality or retention falling is a failure, not a win, and I want that distinguishable rather than hidden inside a headline number. Scope to self-serve SMB, where the evidence actually holds.
